books.title: The Word for World Is Forest
books.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
books.review:
About 80 pages in, I stopped and thought for a second: this is awfully similar to the movie, Avatar.

I actually went back to check the publication date fo the book. 1972. And as I read on, it became increasingly clear where James Cameron must have found his inspiration. I love Avatar. I thought it had such depth: wonderful character writing, great dialogue, meaning, surprises, and so much packed into a heartfelt, deeply moving story. It’s probably among my top ten movies of all time.

But reading Le Guin’s book made me appreciate just how powerful the original idea was. 1972! What a pheonomenal read this is. Le Guin has this extraordinary ability to enchant you, to pull you into a world where you don’t understand some of the words, phrases or customs, but you stay with her because you she's building something magical. (Or as the Gen Z's say, 'let her cook', and boy, she cooked)

You start caring about the Athsheans, these small green, hairy creatures who seem to have so little, yet have so much to teach us about a planet and what it means to belong to one. Beautiful prose, such great writing, and a magical way to tell human beings that there is more to aspire for than our eternal greed. And the idea that the forest is the most revered, sanctimonious thing that we should conserve and protect, and everything else comes secondary. Written in 1972, and somehow still painfully relevant in 2026. This is a truly special book, and now among my favourite works of fiction. HIGLY RECOMMEND

books.title: Mountains of Fire: The Menace, Meaning, and Magic of Volcanoes
books.author: Clive Oppenheimer
books.review:
This is a book of two halves. The first half is fantastic. Oppenheimer explores volcanoes as objects of immense fascination: why are we drawn to them, the myths we build around them, how different cultures revere them, and the stories that make them larger than life. Volcanoes are magical creatures with scientific processes and cultural artefacts passed on from generations. Their science is unexplored, even till date: how exactly do eruptions work, how can scientists measure and monitor them, what can we learn about our young planet from volcanic activity et al... Then the book loses me.

The final hundred pages increasingly read like a diary of the people Oppenheimer met and the work they were involved in. There are so many names, places and trite anecdotes, I eventually lost track of who was who and, more importantly, lost interest in why I was reading about them.

I wish the book had stayed with the magic of volcanoes: more science, more mythology, more stories about why these mountains have captivated humans for millennia. Instead, it becomes a record of travels and acquaintances.

If you’re genuinely interested in geology and volcanology, there’s plenty here to enjoy. For everyone else, this falls prey to what makes a good book great: a stern editor.

books.title: Forces of Nature
books.author: Brian Cox
books.review: Another stunning exploration of the planet we inhabit. Told in Brian Cox's quintessentially curious voice, i loved this reading of science and the scientists who do what they do. He does not shy away from getting deeply technical to explain simple concepts — my only grouse was i wish these concepts were two notches simpler, and three notches more interesting to let the reader sink their teeth into hundreds of these concepts. There's a lot of biting humour and a solid exploration to make science more accessible for all, just missed the mark to be riveting enough. It's a simple, and easy read and the first 30 pages are beautifully rendered. Read it, because it's easy, and with enough diligence and your own curiosity to pursue rabbit holes defined in the book, you might just enjoy it more than i did.

books.title: Glorious Exploits
books.author: Ferdia Lennon
books.review:
The Goodreads description for this book is the best pitch for a book I've ever read. Two potters taming a legion of defeated soldiers into putting on a play. Incredible. I ordered the book immediately.

I really wanted this book to live up to the promise of that premise and, in doing so, topple my all time favourite: Paul Beatty's, The Sellout. That was the benhcmark of biting satire, and one that made me actually laugh reading fantastic prose.

It didn’t quite get there.
But, comparison is the thief of Joy, Roosevelt once remarked. And that loss was felt as i greedily read the final 50 pulsating pages, to realise this book ebbs and flows

Glorious Exploits has a clean, compelling storyline. It’s an easy read, and a terrific debut. I only wish the one-liners had more bite, the prose had more teeth, and the satire made me a little more uncomfortable. After all, there were all the elements in there to make this book a hysterical riot. I found it somewhat staid at different parts.

But if you truly strip away comparisons, it stands very well on its own, more so as a debut.

There are moments of great beauty and genuine emotion, and I particularly enjoyed the character arcs. There is something deeply compelling about the underdog, about someone who has lost their way and, finds it again. I also loved the rabbit holes it opened up into Euripides and the many characters of Greek mythology. Whenever the book dragged, those little excursions into the world behind the story were a welcome respite.

Overall, I’d recommend this if you want a quick fix: a fantastic premise, and a nail-biting page-turner in its last 50-pages: a great example of what good fiction should be.

books.title: Foster
books.author: Claire Keegan
books.review:
WHAT. A. BOOK!

Hardly 100-pages long, yet, its word-to-feel ratio is off the charts. It's a breezy story of an unnamed young girl who finds self-worth in a foster family. It transports you inside rural Ireland, and a phenomenally poignant read.

Highly recommend.

books.title: The Loneliness of Sonia and Sunny
books.author: Kiran Desai
books.review:
Extraordinary prose, acerbically funny, frequently piercing, and a deep exploration of the emotional construct of Indian families. This was a fun read, even if it's 700-pages long.

The novel explores the subconscious undercrurrents beneath relationships: between husbands and wives, parents and children, and families strung together by affection, ego, resentment, duty, and frustartion. Desai gives voice to thoughts people don't like to admit, exposing the suppressed insecurities, and contradictions that shape how we behave with those closest to us. At a lot parts, the prose feels uncomfortably raw and candid.

Although the book follows an the central relationship between Sonia and Sunny, its real subject is its people. At nearly 700 pages, it can feel sprawling, yet the length allows its characters to emerge with remarkable depth. Desai unpeals their souls and in many ways makes you think of a relative or friend who mimics these characters.

There are pockets of romance, mysticism, and magical realism, which evoke an enchanting idea of India. And to be honest, the country is rendered through what feels like an outsider’s gaze, as though cultural India has never grown from its yoke of supression. (nitpicking here)

This is a novel that conquers what loneliness is, the many trepidations of family, identity, and the contradictory ways in which we love, hate and learn to live with the many people in our lives. (We all have that one friend)

Read it when you have the luxury of time, because this is a book of inviting prose, and one of envy — oh, what i would give to be able to think and write like Kiran Desai :(

books.title: The Unbearable Lightness of Being
books.author: Milan Kundera
books.review:
Every once in a while you come across a book with exquisite prose, peppered with the right dose of philosophy, history & a plot circling the perpetual quest for happiness; that's the 'unbearable lightness of *our* being'.

It's so sublime in its imagery and showcases so much nuance of human emotion abstaining from basic logic. In fact, this dichotomy of logic and emotion is what makes us such wildly fascinating creatures, and Kundra intellectualises this in such astute fashion, i devoured this book 😊

Delectable. Highly recommend. ❤️

books.title: Abundance
books.author: Ezra Klein
books.review:
The most defining book of our times. it gives us a language to understand the liberalism fiasco—where they've gotten so good at saying the right things, without doing anything. It's easier to be a fence-sitter than a doer.

The act of creation attracts detractors by nature, but we need builders & doers to out-think any crisis: from affordability to the climate.

The book explains the need for serendipity, unleashing capital on scientific progress, and using the best & worst of capitalism to fight the planet's most pressing causes. It's a sobering, yet hopeful read.

books.title: Climate Capitalism: Winning the Global Race to Zero Emissions
books.author: Akshat Rathi
books.review:
As a climate tech newbie, I thoroughly enjoyed Akshat Rathi's book.

It stitches together policy, people, companies and countries, shaping a once-in-a-generation opportunity to reverse decades of climate inaction.

Highly recommended reading.

books.title: Darjeeling: The Colorful History and Precarious Fate of the World's Greatest Tea
books.author: Jeff Koehler
books.review:
A tale flush with history, geography and the romantic allure of the world's most famous tea, and how its conspirators orchestrated it all.

The pleasantly astringent writing captures Darjeeling; past, present and the future.

if you want a summary and some key notes from the book: https://adadithya.notion.site/Darjeel...

books.title: The Night Circus
books.author: Erin Morgenstern
books.review:
A dreamy, magical tale of two people, controlled by two others. It's borderline fantasy, but a large part of the story is rooted in reality. I really liked how I could paint a picture of the entire circus and all the little imagery the author has painstakingly crafted. It's a beautiful read on a cold winter night. Fantasy was effectively dead for me after Harry Potter, but this genre of 'bordeline fantasy story rooted in intriguing reality is a welcome respite.

Recommended read :)

books.title: Tomorrow, and Tomorrow, and Tomorrow
books.author: Gabrielle Zevin
books.review:
Decent read, this. Had a lot of promise initially, but chugged along with a weakly held plot.

Would recommend it to folks who are in a slump, and just want to pick something simple, and easy to read.

There's an interesting 'pop-fiction, easy-to-read, woke,' genre that's growing, and Zevin belongs to that lot. It's catchy, and quick, and I guess not my dose of 'literary' works that I crave.

books.title: Moonwalking with Einstein: The Art and Science of Remembering Everything
books.author: Joshua Foer
books.review:
I've learnt so much from this book. SO MUCH!

One of my most important ones is to conjure absurd, fantastical, maybe even vulgar visual imagery, to create a "memory palace" — allowing me to retain knowledge and improve memory.

Truly a fantastical read.

books.title: An Immense World: How Animal Senses Reveal the Hidden Realms Around Us
books.author: Ed Yong
books.review: A tad hard to plough through, but this book is a revelation. The whole concept of an Umwelt and its broad ramifications is insane. I just wish it were a lot more accessible, and written for the average reader. Some portions were winding, and boring. But overall, this is a fantastic book to learn from and be cognisant of the millions of species around you.

books.title: The Covenant of Water
books.author: Abraham Verghese
books.review:
What an absolute delight this book is. So rich in prose, so vivid in imagination, I laughed & cried reading this towering piece of art.

Is 700+ pages long, & I wished it were a 1000. For the first time in a while, I didn't want a book to end.

The last time I read such a moving piece of fiction was, 'The Kite Runner', and it was deeply moving, this book is in a similar vein. Oprah called this book a Masterpiece, and she's spot on.

Highly recommend.

books.title: User Friendly: How the Hidden Rules of Design Are Changing the Way We Live, Work, and Play
books.author: Cliff Kuang
books.review:
I absolutely loved reading this book on all things design.

It's given me a vocabulary, opened new insights into the thinking of well-designed products, and its astonishingly incredible ramifications.

Highly recommend you pick this tour de force.
Notes on the book - https://adadithya.notion.site/User-Fr...

books.title: Let My People Go Surfing: The Education of a Reluctant Businessman
books.author: Yvon Chouinard
books.review:
"Growth and expansion are values not basic to this corporation."

A terrific read on Patagonia — a company attempting to rewrite rules on how corporate organizations should function.
From caring about the environment, to its people-first policies, and radical ideas on production, this has been a one-of-a-kind read.

Highly recommended.

I loved reading some of the more radical thinking the author has delved into:

The Kosch brothers and Donald Trump's of the business world are heroes to no one except other Businessman with similar values.

We let our customers tell us how much we should grow each year.
Some years it could be 5% growth or 25% which happened during the middle of the Great Recession. Consumers become very conservative during recessions. They stop buying fashionable silly things. They will pay more for a product that is practical, multifunctional and will last a long time. We thrive during recessions.

Repair as a radical act:
As individual consumers, the single best thing we can do for the planet is to keep our stuff in use longer. The simple act of extending the life of our garments through proper care and repair reduces the need to buy more over time, thereby avoiding the carbon dioxide emissions, waste output and water usage required to build the new products.

We live in a culture where replacement is king. These conditions create a society of product consumers, not owners, and there's a difference. Owners are empowered to take responsibility for their purchases, from proper cleaning to repairing, reusing, and sharing. Consumers take, make, dispose of, and repeat, a pattern that is driving us toward ecological bankruptcy.

books.title: A Confederacy of Dunces
books.author: John Kennedy Toole
books.review:
John Kennedy Toole committed suicide at 32. He got depressed after multiple publishers rejected, ‘A Confederacy of Dunces’. His mother managed to find an eminent author who gave her a hearing. That singular event gave us a bewilderingly bewitching Ignatius Reilly — a character that deserves as much recognition as a Mr. Holmes, Atticus Finch or Mr. Gatbsy. Mr. Toole was posthumously awarded the 1981 Pulitzer prize for fiction. And what a deserved award it is.

It’s hard to describe books like, ‘A Confederacy of Dunces’. I suspect in a year or two, I would struggle to recall the ‘storyline’, if you could even call it one. What it is, is fine literature. It’s a book woven with rich language, and tugs at a reader’s intrigue to understand how Mr. Toole manages to keep a plot alive with his spectacular prose. To be clear, there is a storyline. This is not quite your typical meandering Murakami where words spill over a page without rationale, or a linear set of events. You follow a path Mr. Toole has laid out, just that it simply does not matter.

What does count is his language, his use of prose, his era of writers that we don’t produce anymore. His command over the language, his daring challenge to readers to love a misanthrope, an anti-hero who is repulsive, and yet, you want to prod on. That’s what makes this book such a delight.

Through his characters, Mr. Toole implores you to read more, but also, he’s being cunning about it — do you really want to know more about De Consolatione Philosophiae, from a deranged man who struggles with conventional society? He’s having his share of fun, probing the reader.

Mr. Toole must’ve thought:

‘I’m going to use a lunatic character to tell you about Boethius, the late Roman who had written Consolatione. I’m going to walk my reader through rota Fortunae — a wheel of Fortune, a blind goddess who spins humans on a wheel, so luck comes in cycles.’

Mr. Toole would’ve been a fantastic man to converse with, one who trolls you without knowing you’re being trolled. Like the one moment one of his characters says, “Her body had always amazed her. She received it free of charge, yet she had never bought anything that had helped her as much as that body had.” Or this gem of a line, when a character looks at his tablets and calls it, “gems of nihilism”. Or maybe, this line — “Like Harriet Beecher Stowe, Mynra was still around to offend.” What an inventive, fiendishly brilliant troll, Mr Toole would’ve made ;)

And there are enough gems in this book to be sure.

💡 “Apparently I lack some particular perversion which today’s employer is seeking.”

💡 “You could tell by the way he talked, though, that he had gone to school a long time. That was probably what was wrong with him.”

💡 “I refuse to “look up.” Optimism nauseates me. It is perverse. Since man’s fall, his proper position in the universe has been one of misery.”

Who is the dunce really? His brilliantly conjured character, or the reader assimilating this tour de force of a book? Good satire, like any art form, makes you think, debate, and has many interpretations. The sheer audacity of this book made me smile. It’s been a pleasure reading Mr. Toole’s work, and I’m terribly sad we’ll never get to know what wonders he would’ve made had he persisted.

Read A Confederacy of Dunces. It’s biting prose, ingenious dialogue, unlike anything you’ll read. After all, one could always contend, with the proliferation of social media, and a large mike with people who probably should never wield one, we’re at the peak of… well… ‘A confederacy of dunces’ 😉

books.title: Neuromancer (Sprawl, #1)
books.author: William Gibson
books.review: Gave up after 150 pages. Was meandering and convoluted.

books.title: The Vegetarian
books.author: Han Kang
books.review:
Some books make you so uncomfortable, they're almost palpable. You feel your skin crawl as you read. You want to turn to the next page, because you want to know 'what happens next'. But you also don't want to know more, you're in this weird quagmire of where the author is taking you, and you feel supremely uneasy. Good prose can do that. Because readers have this innate ability to vividly paint a picture, conjure the world the author commands, it's an eerie feeling to read uncomfortable realities.

The Vegetarian is that cultural powerhouse. It's a Korean book. It's culture. It's about women, representation, and choice; rather, the illusion of choice. Funny thing; there's no word for vegans in Korean, and that sums up the book.

The main character does not have much of a say in the book, and that's deliberate. A review for the book quotes Jean-Paul Sarte — "Existence precedes essence." You exist, then create the essence to your existence. What if your essence is stripped though?

The stifling of choice, words, power to communicate, express — when someone snatches that away, what does that make you? Who are you? What do you stand for? What's your voice?

The Vegetarian is Kafakesque, with a splash of wandering Murakami, and strong cultural undertones of women and representation.

It's irritating, it's annoying, it's powerful, it's frustrating, and when you have this concoction of emotions while reading prose; the author has succeeded. You, as a reader, have lived through that writing; and that's good literature.

books.title: The Anarchy: The East India Company, Corporate Violence, and the Pillage of an Empire
books.author: William Dalrymple
books.review:
Finally finished this towering book on the most insane corporate organisation ever created in the history of our times. It tracks everything about the East India Company, how it grew so large, the wars it fought, and how the stars aligned to make it the most marauding corporate empire ever built.

It's an absolutely riveting read, written in classic Darlymple style. Read it.

books.title: The Unusual Billionaires
books.author: Saurabh Mukherjea
books.review: 6 profiles of India Inc. A tad winding, but there are really cool stories to devour. The one on Astral and Page Industries was particularly good

books.title: A Case of Exploding Mangoes
books.author: Mohammed Hanif
books.review: One-liners, sarcasm and a punch in the gut story. Great work in all.

books.title: Death's End (Remembrance of Earth’s Past, #3)
books.author: Liu Cixin
books.review: And the remembrance of the earth series concludes in some fashion. Again, 150 pages was meandering and hard to get through, but am glad i saw this through eventually. Stunning book, and a fitting end to a memorable piece of fiction.

books.title: The Dark Forest (Remembrance of Earth’s Past, #2)
books.author: Liu Cixin
books.review: Jesus, what an achievement this book is. There's a 70-age lull (like all of his books), but the conceptualisation and imagination of his storytelling is maddeningly stunning. Throughlyg enjoyed a peek into Cixin Liu's brain and this magic world he's summoned with a stroke of his pen. This has to be one of my favourite books in the last 2 years or so. highly recommended.

books.title: The Three-Body Problem (Remembrance of Earth’s Past, #1)
books.author: Liu Cixin
books.review:
Not a Sci-Fi person. I've read a couple, but none really stuck. After being pestered by multiple people, decided to give this one a shot. This is certainly a life-changing book. It's wildly imaginative, and so well written. It reads like a racy thriller and has enough WTF moments. The beauty of The Three-Body problem is that it also sends you on a wild google goose chase. It implores you to read more, learn more about the planet you live in. I've learnt so many concepts and been awed at how much there is to know. It's fiction, but i've come out wiser, and that's the mark of a good book.

Above all, don't read about this book online, don't try to understand the synopsis. Just begin. It's so spectacularly bold and imaginative, the mind boggles. If you want more reason to pick it up, George R Marin recommends it, Barack Obama loved it. That should suffice. Still not convinced? The makers of Game of THrones want to do a TV show about the book. Yeah, it's bloody good.

Read it, you'll thank me later.

books.title: Pachinko
books.author: Min Jin Lee
books.review:
I was itching for some good fiction and Pachinko was the perfect answer. It's deeply moving, and written with so much compassion, you can't help but want to read more. I devoured this book and fell in love with Min Jin Lee and her characters.

Pachinko is borderline historical fiction. It's about Koreans in Japan. These cultural idiosyncrasies and societal marginalisation get lost in the footnotes of history - more so when there are bigger historic events from 1900-2000s. This book was an eye-opener. The rigidity of cultures, social status and the indomitable Asian spirit culminate into a fantastic read.

Above all, it touches on the central theme of women and the suffering they have to endure. One could look at this and surmise progress for women's empowerment has been... slow. It's a moving book, and written evocatively, Pachinko is a must read.

books.title: The CEO Factory: Management Lessons from Hindustan Unilever
books.author: Sudhir Sitapati
books.review:
This is a fantastic book on a company that touches 9 out of 10 households and yet, few no about its origins or Hindustan Unilever. But say Surf, Rin, Taj tea or Brooke Bond and you'll know it all. There are some fascinating stories from the man who's been there, done that. You should take it with a pinch of salt because Sudhir is still working at HUL, but the range of anecdotal stories on HUL's modus operandi is incredibly fantastic. It's a delightful read and one that'll make you appreciate what it takes to build products and, more importantly, cultures.

I don't want to give away too much, but this is an essential read to understand a company close to Indians.

books.title: A Gentleman in Moscow
books.author: Amor Towles
books.review:
What an absolutely charming book this is. This ranks right up there among my all time favourite books and certainly will be one of the finest books I read in 2020.

Picture this: The entire book is about one man ordered to be in a house arrest in a hotel for his entire life. It's 450+ pages long with size 9 font. IF that sounds miserable, you're in for a shock. Amor Towels is a splendidly gifted writer and this book is testimonial to the power of writing. His character keeps you gripped the entire journey and you're left desperately wanting more. Mind you, it's not preachy by any means, it's just such an eloquently written book, it makes you wonder how Towels managed it all.

If there's one book you want to read in 2020, this is it. If you're stuck at home and the spirits are waning, this book will do the trick. It's no wonder Bill Gates recommended it as one of his favourites. Pick it up, you're in for a treat and will definitely put a smile on your face. :)

books.title: No Logo
books.author: Naomi Klein
books.review:
I typically don't read books on branding and marketing. Most of these have reams of unnecessary gibberish. But when i stumbled on Naomi Klein's book, i picked it up on a whim. This book was released in 1999 - the rules of 'brand' had changed since then, or so i thought. After all, we live in a world where social media networks are toppling democracies and there's no mention of 'digital advertising' on the book at all. Imagine a marketing book without even a mention of digital advertising! Blasphemy. But this was 1999. And 1999 was between the Mad Men and The Zuck. It was also when a growing tide of consumers started getting a lot more conscious about what they consume.

I read the synopsis and one commentator claimed Klein to be the heiress to Chomsky. Big shoes to fill and thus, I began. This was my journey into understanding the foe; rather, how to hoodwink one as a brand marketer. What followed was a stunning revelation into the extend brands go to corner their market and the means they undertake. There are a few actionable insights in there too, but above all, it speaks about a time when brands had to reinvent themselves to stay relevant. And today's 'corporate activism' gusto was one that was sowed a long long time ago.

It made me think - For profitability in the new world order, activism has to be ingrained in the ethos of a brand. That was a humongous learning reading New Logo and its deep insights into the troubles many brands underwent to get where they are now. And no, brands don't have to believe in what they do, as long as they can convince the rest they care. It's profoundly capitalistic and deviously brilliant. Good read really - more so if you want to understand marketing and want to build a brand.

books.title: Watchmen
books.author: Alan Moore
books.review: Kicking myself for not picking this up when multiple friends, acquaintances told me to read it. I've never read a graphic novel and always thought I can't warm up to it. But this is no ordinary book. Watchmen has so many layers to it. The language is sublime, the wit is a miss if you're not paying attention, the characterisation is nuanced, the storyline is meticulous and above all, this is not a book you parse through. You pause. You Google obscure references to history, music, art and literature. It's a towering book that demands your attention long after you've finished it. The kind of book that'll prod you do get on the internet, read fan theories and interpretations. An absolute treat and one that's going to keep me coming back for more.

books.title: Homegoing
books.author: Yaa Gyasi
books.review: Probably one of the finest historical fictions i've ever read. Moving, shocking and an absolute page-turner of a book.

books.title: The Hard Thing About Hard Things: Building a Business When There Are No Easy Answers―Straight Talk on the Challenges of Entrepreneurship
books.author: Ben Horowitz

books.title: Norse Mythology
books.author: Neil Gaiman
books.review:
If you've ever wanted a quick, short and simple read on Norse mythology, this is the book to pick-up. The prose is easy, the writing is sharp and in the hands of a master storyteller, Odin Loki and Thor come alive. In quintessential Gaiman style, 'Norse Mythology' is a page turner. It's 8-10 short stories about the gods and how they came to be.

Think of Gaiman's book as an encyclopedia of sorts. This is a reference book that tells you the most important stories in the Norse mythology and tells them with persuasion. It covers the entire gamut of characters and written for anyone and everyone. I particularly enjoyed the way Gaiman adds descriptions and emphasis to characters in subsequent chapters, despite mentioning them in previous ones.

There are a hundred names from goats and bulls to hammers and horns, so recalling them all can get a tad difficult and Gaiman does a fabulous job of reminding you of it all.

books.title: The Hidden Pool
books.author: Ruskin Bond
books.review: Reminded me of school and family. Wasn't a water body dad and me wouldn't jump into. He'd first survey, and then i'd go in. I've jumped into more water bodies than I can count now. ❤️

books.title: The Forty Rules of Love
books.author: Elif Shafak
books.review:
The bar for Turkish authors is high. Extremely high. A Nobel laureate-kind of high. *cough* Orhan Pamuk *cough*. The Forty Rules of Love promises a lot, but doesn't deliver. At its heart, it's a tale of a wandering dervish meeting Rumi before Rumi was Rumi. What it becomes, is a ramble around morals, values and a heady concotion of pithy self-help. And that's sad, because as a plot, it's a fascinating one - how Rumi transforms, his steady march to becoming a poet.

After about 200 pages, I paused and realised Elif Shafak's tale is a self-help book packaged under the guise of fiction. I was looking for a story, flowing language, a tale - but got none of it. For someone as endlessly fascination as Rumi, this book does a great disservice to the legend.

books.title: Sapiens: A Brief History of Humankind
books.author: Yuval Noah Harari
books.review:
There was more than one species of humans living at the same time, and over the course of 2.4 million years, Homo Sapiens destroyed and pillaged not just other human species, but thousands of animals and plants and other living beings. With those first few lines, the history of our species starts with the indelible stain of destructors par excellence. Homo Sapiens have presided over the largest mass murdering of life on earth and here we stand; triumphant and proud of what humanity stands for. Harari's book is a challenge, an anticlimax to how we got where we are and how can learn to improve, and it doesn't disappoint.

The first 150-pages of Harari's Sapiens is a whirlwind ride. Writing the history of our species for a mass audience is no easy task and it's no surprise this book is a bestseller. It ticks all the right boxes. Anyone can read it and walk away wiser - and that's the pulse of a non-fiction book. For me, page 90-onwards was an absorbing insight into how deep the author has probed and preyed and taken a stand on the most controversial subjects.

How can one critique the advent of agriculture? It seemed impossible, and yet, Harari's account of the onslaught of wheat on Homo Sapiens, is a terrific read. There is a generalisation to be made around how Luxuries eventually become necessities and it isn't off the mark. The very nature of evolution from systemic farming to the bare 'necessity' of having a smartphone dictates today's luxuries are tomorrow's necessities. Here's an author who writes evocatively, not shy to voice his own view point and speaks to the reader. For this and for this alone, Sapiens is a must read for anyone. You will come out knowing more, being more mindful of the world around you and that's a win for me.

Where it failed - the last 100-pages were preachy, spoke in length about religion, the nature of happiness etc... Topics that needed objectivity and perhaps not in a book that had so much more to offer. But that's just me. Read it, for you seldom come across such a commanding author who writes for all to read, understand and imbibe.

books.title: How Google Works
books.author: Eric Schmidt
books.review: Some interesting titbits in there with solid examples. My main grouse with books such as these: Need more real life examples, ideas are way too macro. But this one in particular tackled some of those problems. The book keeps the reader engaged, is not overtly preachy and has some lessons for all. My one big problem: It makes you believe engineers are god's gift to mankind. But that's understandable when the author is so devoted to his job. Take things with a pinch of salt. More than anything, it gives you a glimpse (however one-sided it might be) of how the big folks in tech think, act. Read it.

books.title: The Undoing Project: A Friendship That Changed Our Minds
books.author: Michael Lewis
books.review:
This was a bitter pill to swallow. I love Michael Lewis. And I cribbed through this book. I had half a mind to take it to the barn and shoot it, but endured till the last pages. Lewis takes complex subjects and simplifies them; it's what makes an outsider love his work. Anyone can pickup 'Flash Boys' and be amazed by the world of high frequency trading. The Big Short was revered for its ability to connect with a broader audience. And yet, The Undoing Project fell well short of its own lofty credentials. This was a classic case of the author's reputation getting the better of him. After all, this certainly is a story worth narrating. An important story at that. This was the friendship that set the course for economics and psychologists working together, and yet, it's treatment was for a small subset of an audience.

Books are for all. Books inform, educate, simplify the complex so one can learn and be amazed. The Undoing Project promised friendship, but gave me a lot of grief. I simply didn't get it. Some were long rants, some too complex and not dumbed down, some were just way too boring. I laboured through it all. This book was supposed to tell us the birth of behavioural economics, how accidents are closely linked to speaking on cell phones while driving, how a generation of psychologists framed economics and yet, for all the hope it carried, it was well short of an informative read.

Was this supposed to be for students studying advanced economics or psychologists doing advanced studies? If it was, I'm sure it only scratched the surface. The book was an in-between. Neither for specialists, nor beginners. In all, i was disappointed. Read it if you have to.

books.title: Deep Thinking: Where Machine Intelligence Ends and Human Creativity Begins
books.author: Garry Kasparov

books.title: The Red-Haired Woman
books.author: Orhan Pamuk
books.review:
I don’t ‘review’ books. I’m not skilled at it, nor am I good at judging the quality of a person’s labour. I haven’t even read as much to be qualified to have much of an opinion. I merely try to help someone else make a decision on whether they should read a book or not. With that in mind, Pamuk’s ‘The red-haired woman’ is a difficult one to assess. I don’t know what I feel about it. Am I judging the book based on reading the author’s past works? Pamuk’s latest is an enigma of sorts. And yet, it taught me something on the idea of reading books.

When I read ‘Brave New world’, I vowed never to read a dystopian novel again. It was disturbing. It was painful and all too real. Yet, it is one of the most brilliant books I’ve ever read. It’s similar to watching Anthony Brugees’ ‘A Clockwork Orange’ - one of the most brilliant movies ever made, yet utterly distasteful and psychotic.

I’ve read a lot of Pamuk and I love his breezy narration. The language flows and you relate so well to the Nobel prize winning author. He keeps it simple, touches you when you least expect it and is an absolute delight. The red-haired woman doesn’t have those lines; that language that makes you empathise, makes you want to pause and look out the window, take a deep breath and let those words drown inside you, making you feel what it’s like to let words, sentences and paragraphs soothe you and amaze everything that’s beautiful about this very moment.

I finished the book, enjoying some portions, completely losing on others. Maybe that’s the journey of reading a good book – to be able to lose yourself a bit, to not want to ‘rate’ a book, to not know what you feel like, yet to have learnt something from that experience. The red-haired woman, like its title, is a mystery. And that’s why I love reading. This feeling of nothingness; that means a lot more in an age where we compartmentalize things in the good or the bad.

With that absolutely non-helpful 300 words, comes the big question, should you read Pamuk? (my real objective of ‘reviewing’ books is to help others make a decision!!)

I DON’T KNOW.

And if that tells you something, maybe you should read it or maybe you should move on.

books.title: Serious Men
books.author: Manu Joseph
books.review:
Sardonic. Dismissive. Scornful. Wry. Contempt. Manu Joseph. All same things really. His debut ‘Serious Men’ is quintessential Manu. There is a vituperative outburst in the book that’s palpable. You wouldn’t be too surprised to realise this is a Manu Joseph book if you’ve read enough of his articles. There’s a lot of wit, social messages, smart one-liners and the familiar vituperative writing that comes with the book. A friend couldn’t read more than a 70 pages because she taught it was cynical. “Too bitter for my taste and I hate the way women are portrayed in the book,” she said.

It’s a good read. It’s also not as ambitious as one would expect. There’s more you want from a journalist/author as cynical as Manu. The plotline is good. The characterisation is envious. You can picture the characters in your mind; how they look dress, even talk and therein lays the author’s command over his craft. It’s no wonder the book won a few awards. It’s no wonder that you’ll most likely read another of his books. This is a book written in 2010, and one can only wonder how much bigger a tussle Manu Joseph now has with the world. He has far more material to tinker with and that means better lines, a sharper plot and a lot of frustration venting on those pages.

Read Serious Men because it’s filled with sentences you’d want to quote. Read it because it’s a nice story to narrate. Read it because you’ll come back thinking, ‘Wow, how can someone hate the world so much?’

books.title: The Color of Magic (Discworld, #1; Rincewind, #1)
books.author: Terry Pratchett
books.review:
In one of Terry Pratchett’s books, "A Slip of the Keyboard” the author himself states that you shouldn’t start with the beginning of the ‘Discworld series’, yet, that’s exactly what I did. Dammit, if only I discussed this with some of my more learned friends. The Colour of Magic is TP’s first book in the Discworld series and for a TP beginner, it gave some insights into why he’s such a distinguished author. Fair disclosure – I don’t like fantasy fiction. I’ve read 5 of the Harry Potter novels and I don't think anyone can beat that. It's my happy bubble and I have no intention of bursting it. I’ve tried 2-3 more fantasy novels, but never enjoyed them much. So, writing this review is probably not fair to the author or his works. Having said that, I’m looking forward to reading more of his works. Nevertheless, there are some takeaways from his first in the series:

There’s a lot of biting sarcasm and humour in the book. TP is wildly imaginative and to conjure the Discworld should take something of a genius and he does this with some gusto. Unfortunately, the book has too many characters who don’t have closure. Some walk right in and you have no idea what happened to them. Therefore, a lot of story plots remain missing. It’s a good ‘comedy of errors’ sort of book with witty one-liners and slapstick humour. But I wish there was a storyline to it all. I was equally frustrated reading about 300+ references to words I have no idea what they mean. I lost the will to google so many of these words that mean something to the author, but the reader is left in the lurch. Lastly, there could’ve been so much more humour, considering the characters he created. The Colour of Magic was a tease – it tells you that Terry Pratchett can only get better and as one of my friends remarked, ‘TP takes some time to get into the groove’ and I shouldn’t be starting with his first in the series. Who knows, I will be revisiting this rant after 2-3 books of his. Verdict – Don’t read it if you haven’t already read 2-3 of this best.

books.title: Flash Boys: A Wall Street Revolt
books.author: Michael Lewis
books.review:
This is the book that shook Wall Street. This is the book that made an entire trading floor halt and stare at a CNBC interview with the author and one of the key protagonists. This is the book that made the Department of Justice and FBI launch an investigation into banks, brokers, traders, funds and the entire financial industry. This is the author that redefined baseball, wrote one of the best financial books that shackled the heels of big banks. (The Big Short) Pardon the dramatization, but I postponed reading this book by a year and I’m still kicking myself for it. Flash Boys will go down as one of history’s most defining books written on modern finance.

If Niall Ferguson told us about the Rothschild and the ascent of money, Michael Lewis shed light on some of the most incredibly lesser known human stories powering the world of Collateralized Debt Obligations, (yeah, that word again), derivatives and High Frequency Traders (HFT). At the heart of it is Lewis’ ability to be a storyteller on complex subjects. He ‘humanises’ the story for an average reader like me to make sense of the convolutions of Wall Street. He dumbs down trading and makes a thriller out of numbers, data, algorithms and machines. The people in his books are his baits – which the author uses to paint the bigger picture; how corrupt is Wall Street?

Flash Boys revolves around HFT. It’s about how few traders profit from the orders placed by others and getting trading data ahead of the source. The difference accounts for billions of dollars being ‘swindled’ by traders with complex algorithms. The book then traces the journey of how a handful of men mount an assault on this injustice in Wall Street, tracking their trials and tribulations. It’s an enthralling read. I only wish it could be a notch more simplified. I shouldn’t be giving away more, but read this brilliant work because it’s one of the best books of non-fiction you will encounter. Read it because it’s about the kind of fraud that makes billionaires and puts hard-working men and women at the vanguard. But above all, read it to be shocked and dazzled.

books.title: The Sellout
books.author: Paul Beatty
books.review:
I've never read anything like this before. Paul Beatty's 'The Sellout' is easily the funniest and most sarcastic book I've ever read. It's witty, it's clever and it's dripping with dark dry humour. From page 1 till the end, this was a bloody riot. I was shocked, appalled, laughed my heart out and was stunned at the author's imagination to conceive and outrageous plot and build the most fascinating characters around this maniacal plot.

Sarah Silverman stated that it was 'like demented angels wrote it' and she is absolutely spot on. It takes a certain audacity to write a book in praise of bringing back slavery and segregating a school and Mr. Beatty does it with a comical genius that I've never come across in my life. And it's not just the nonchalant way in which he writes about 'black' oppression, but the wit in which he goes about building a case. He wasn't preachy the way most authors fall prey to when they write about an important cultural movement.

This book is not a rant; quite the contrary. It's certainly one of the most intelligent works that uses humour as a base to talk about the very notion of racism in the 21st century. As The Guardian remarked, "The longer you stare at Beatty's pages, the smarter you'll get," and I found myself consistently googling references to bloomian dogmatism, scottsboro boys, omphaloskepsis and so much more. The author takes you on a ride, teaching you more, prodding you to understand more and learn about the moment. But what i particularly enjoyed was how he pirouetted the reader into laughing and learning. Read it, because it's funny as hell. Read it, because you'll learn something and be thoroughly entertained. Read it, because it might just be among my top 10 favourite books ever :)

books.title: Malice (Detective Kaga, #1)
books.author: Keigo Higashino
books.review:
I hated the title of the book and it probably has a deeper meaning in Japanese, but Keigo Higashino's Malice is crisp and to the point. It's quite the thriller and keeps you engaged. It's not quite the page turner, but Higashino knows how to weave a tale and spring a surprise. You got to give it to the author for mixing in the right ingredients of making an enthralling read.

Where Higashino fails is in building suspense, absorbing the reader and framing the mystery in a character. I hate comparing authors, but Murakami does this so flawlessly and one would expect that from a Japanese author. Malice is a good read, but it's not one that keeps you on your toes, wanting for more. Read it if you crave for a thriller and have read none in a while. Read it if you want to understand Japanese culture. Read it because it's crisp, simple language and has tells you a little about Japan you wouldn't otherwise know.

books.title: Six of Crows (Six of Crows, #1)
books.author: Leigh Bardugo
books.review: Gripping story with twists and turns. Superb effort to conjure a world filled with flying monsters and drugs that make you superhuman. I liked the book, enjoyed reading portions of it. It wasn't quite in the league of pulsating adrenaline thumping fiction, but it does a decent job. Read it if you absolutely have to, but this is most likely meant for the big screen.

books.title: A Strangeness in My Mind
books.author: Orhan Pamuk
books.review:
Aaah, well.. Sometimes you expect too much from your favourite authors. But despite these expectations, I felt immensely disappointed by Pamuk's 'A Strangeness in My Mind'. Even the most ardent critics will agree that Pamuk's prose is impeccable. His language flows and you immediately get captivated with the way he wraps you in and makes you comfortable with his simple story lines. Let me explain...

Pamuk's 'My Name is Red' is a great story. The book speaks to you. Trees and objects are characters in themselves and the storyline is powerful as much as it's engaging. The 'Museum of Innocence' on the other hand, is a book with a decent storyline but impeccable writing. You want to read every word of the 600+ pages masterpiece, because of its language; the way he weaves the words like a powerful symphony. These are two different books - one that relies on its storytelling, the other on its prose. And I loved both his works.

Pamuk's latest venture falls flat on both ends unfortunately. Neither was the prose lyrical, nor did I particularly enjoy the story. It was 600+ pages of the life of a passionate boza seller, and we get it, but did he really need that gigantic a book to convey Mevlut's thoughts? Meh.

books.title: The Lives of Others
books.author: Neel Mukherjee
books.review:
Reading Neel Mukherjee's 'The Lives of Others' felt like an exploration into the author's own beliefs of India's communist factions. Interlaced with the story of a Calcutta family’s social lives, it traces the symptoms leading up to the Naxalite revolution in 1969. The book is rich in language and seeped in cultural nuances. It's no surprise that it was deemed worthy of a Booker nomination.

Mukherjee’s language is simple, yet powerful and he weaves a simple story with the many superstitions and social dogmas of Indian society. It’s not a roller-coaster ride of a book with plots and sub-plots. He builds characters and gives adequate time to make them impressionable to the reader. The language makes this book a compelling read.

Read it, because it’s about an India you might not have heard much of. It’s about the story of a rich family with bigotry and how one boy left all the luxuries of life to join a movement he believed in.

books.title: The Smoke Is Rising
books.author: Mahesh Rao
books.review:
Mahesh Rao is one to watch out for the future, and that's pretty much the best praise one can summon after reading his first novel. The smoke is rising is promises a lot with its characters and a city's (Mysore) conflict with embracing modernism on the face of historic traditionalism. But like most authors who delve into this subject, it falls well short of unearthing the complexities of its characters.

The language is good, his style of conjuring a physical location is notable and he builds a thought, but ultimately, the plot plummets and doesn't grip the readers' attention. The book has its moments, but I can't think of one chapter or page I would like to talk about or praise. But there is hope, should Mahesh work on his story telling capabilities.

Read it if you absolutely must, else there are other books to chose from.

books.title: A Long Way Gone: Memoirs of a Boy Soldier
books.author: Ishmael Beah
books.review:
Ishmael Beah is a murderer. He slit a boy's throat when he was about 15 years old. None of this is his fault; the war shaped him, the consequences of a stranger's violence engulfed him and his helplessness is palpable.

A long way gone is the story of a boy and his indoctrination into violence and drugs. After his college mates kept referring to him being in the war as "cool," 27 year old Ishmael wrote on of non-fictions best books. Narrated from the heart with simple prose and a touching story of life and its fragility, this is deservedly among the Top 50 non-fiction books you must read in your life!

A paraphrased story at the end of the book that moved me to tears -

A hunter went into a bush to kill a monkey. On seeing him, the monkey said, 'If you shoot me, your father will die, if you don't, your mother will.'
It's a story often said during rituals in the village and no one could answer it. Today, if someone asks me, I'd say, I would shoot the monkey and lose my father, so it would know longer have a chance to put others in the same predicament.

Must read.

books.title: White Mughals
books.author: William Dalrymple
books.review:
William Dalrymple writes evocatively and his research is immaculate as much as it's painstaking. He pieces together a story of love between a British resident and a Persian muslim from mere letters and few documents, and this is highly commendable.

While he takes lot of pain to explain the prevalence of inter-marriages between the Brits and the Indians even before the 17th century, he gets a little carried away with the magnitude of the task in hand. I really thought the book could be about 100 pages shorter. There's a fairly long rant about gardens and the kind of plants the Brits longed for. A dozen other irrelevant characters creep in and out of the book without adding value to the story.
While I appreciate the bulid-up to the central tale, the narration gets a tad winded while portraying the sincerity of the love between Kirkpatrick and Khar-ul-Nissa.

Nevertheless, this a towering piece of non-fiction and much credit must be given to Dalrymple for unearthing important source documents and recreating a fascinating and binding love story in the 18th century. It's an intriguing tale of how the Brits went from India's neigbourly friends to bitter enemies.

Dalrymple gives much to ponder, had Kirkpatrick and gentlemen of his refined generation survived, would've the British lasted longer? Would’ve the Brits changed the framework of their treaties, which merely intended to bankrupt the existing rulers and bring discord? James Kirkpatrick did have the power to shape policy of British India in the latter years had he survived.
As a rule, historians don't speculate and form opinions, but this story is as much about the affair, as the subsequent events which led to shaping India in the 18th and 19th century.

books.title: Freakonomics: A Rogue Economist Explores the Hidden Side of Everything
books.author: Steven D. Levitt

books.title: Monk Who Sold His Ferrari: A Remarkable Story About Living Your Dreams
books.author: Robin Sharma
books.review: BRILLIANT. PROFOUND. INSPIRATIONAL. Its impossible to review such a fabulous book.

books.title: In Spite Of The Gods
books.author: Edward Luce
books.review:
A comprehensive book on India that covers EVERYTHING on its way from politics to the people and comparisons with our envious neighbours. Edward Luce's work and research is highly commendable. A must read book for people who want to know the story of India and why India is a nation that is on the threshold of greatness despite its plethora of limitations.

The story of India is a unique one as a fair percent of the population are unaware and remain oblivious to the fact that India might just be able to achieve super power status in due time.

Drawing quotes from Amartya Sen, Abdul Kalam, Sonia Gandhi, Advani and various eminent figures the book gives a full fledge view on India's failures and India's strong points.

books.title: The Glass Palace
books.author: Amitav Ghosh
books.review:
Easily among The Top 5 non-fiction storytelling books I've ever read. Highly recommended reading for anyone who loves history and a good story of the days of the colonial Empire. The climax of the Empire is usually woven with India's defiant visionary, Mahatma Gandhi, and his unique methods of non-violence to cast out a 200 year old colonial superpower. The little stories of Burma and the chaos it faced post Britain and its struggle for democracy have been ignored and almost unheard of. Ghosh's story is a telling tale of this struggle and its people.

Amitav Ghosh's fabulously grand story is a deep, poignant and a touching tale that sings like an ode to humanity.

books.title: Freedom at Midnight
books.author: Dominique Lapierre
books.review: The song of India. Relive India and its obnoxious Maharajahs. If you haven't read this magnum opus larger than life delight, you haven't read much.

books.title: Surely You're Joking, Mr. Feynman!: Adventures of a Curious Character
books.author: Richard P. Feynman

books.title: My Diamond Days With Osho
books.author: Ma Prem Shunyo
books.review:
Preachy. Bad grammar. Picked up the book to read and know more about Osho. The book failed miserably in terms of portraying what Osho stood for and his ideas. Though i learnt a few key points and what Osho stood for. The author intended to make it more personal and how her fame sky rocketed being associated with Osho. A complete lack of knowledge on politics and she exposes her naivety when she talks about India and other religions.

Does capture a few dear talks of Osho and what he wanted the world to know. I suggest you pick up a book written by Osho himself. Read it if you must and have absolutely nothing to do other than watch a soap ;-)

books.title: India After Gandhi: The History of the World's Largest Democracy
books.author: Ramachandra Guha
books.review: A towering book such as this one needs an exhaustive review. Will post one in a while.

books.title: The Colour of Law (Scott Fenny, #1)
books.author: Mark Gimenez
books.review: The second worst book I've ever read. Gut sucked in with the "NEXT GRISHAM" advertising ploy. If you ever need tips on how NOT TO WRITE A NOVEL, this book serves as good fodder.

books.title: The World Is Flat: A Brief History of the Twenty-first Century
books.author: Thomas L. Friedman

books.title: Reluctant Fundamentalist
books.author: Mohsin Hamid
books.review:
The Reluctant Fundamentalist is a book that I managed to finish in two days despite being busy. Its an amazingly sharp and well-written book. For the ones who swear on literary power, Hamid satisfies the need. For the ones looking for a good story with a pacy narrative, will not be disappointed.

Honest is the word I would use to describe the book in a nutshell. The pain of the lead character is palpable as he narrates his story. The brevity of the author is going to make him a man to watch out for.

books.title: The God of Small Things
books.author: Arundhati Roy
books.review: If you want a compendium of metaphors, look no further that Arundathi Roy's distasteful sham of a book. If that may sound rude to you, i recommend the reader to read The God of Small things. An apt title to the book would be, Small Things.

books.title: Empire: The Rise and Demise of the British World Order and the Lessons for Global Power
books.author: Niall Ferguson
books.review:
Its very hard to talk about the pros of colonialism and imperialism. The burgeoning growth of the EMPIRE; Britain and the marvels of how a select civilization managed to control nearly the entire world.

Purely for history lovers who are fascinated with the mysteries of an Empire which rose from ashes and ultimately crumbled. Or did it?

An articulation of History's prodigal daughter ; BRITAIN.

books.title: Eats, Shoots & Leaves: The Zero Tolerance Approach to Punctuation
books.author: Lynne Truss

books.title: The Lover
books.author: Marguerite Duras
books.review:
A book. A poem. A provocative ode.
The Lover, is... A tyrst with life's whims.

books.title: Blink: The Power of Thinking Without Thinking
books.author: Malcolm Gladwell

books.title: Embers
books.author: Sándor Márai
books.review: That was a painful read overall. Was assaulted by metaphors and tonnes of Deepak Chopra like advice about anything and everything. This might be a classic, but a total dud for me. 🙏

books.title: The Shadow Lines
books.author: Amitav Ghosh
books.review:
Sublime, yet powerful. Gosh's Shadow Lines talks about the insignificance and banality of national boundaries.

Never felt so moved by a book since I read Hosseini's, Kite Runner. Ghosh connects criss crossing timelines between Calcutta, London and Dhaka into a beautiful moral.

It is a book whose characters you glide with until the very end when they come alive and narrate a somber tale of nationhood.

Read it for its fluidity and above all, over a cup of tea, with your thinking cap on.

books.title: Such a Long Journey
books.author: Rohinton Mistry
books.review:
Mistry's prose is an absolute delight. He has humor and his physical description is worth savoring. The book revolves around the politics of the 70's and largely centers around the 1971 Nagarwala scandal. Remember that? Indira's easy access to the RBI and 'Bangladeshi babu'... ?

Such a long journey is the same book that got into controversy with Bal Thackeray's grandson. Though there are some casual references (factual) to the MNS' ways, hard to see why the grandson wanted to ban Mistry 19s work.

If anyone, the INC should have gotten mad about the book and Mistry's description of a country in the wane.

Read the book for its simple and easy-to-read prose, and the Mistry's way of narrating the simplest incident. My favourite part is the way in which he describes a tale in a brothel in about 3 pages. You will know it when you read it. Super stuff.

To sum it up, here is a simple explanation of the author I found in The Guardian --

"Mistry is a writer who 19s interested in telling stories . . . stories about the human heart and the human mind and of how we all struggle in this world, whether we are migrants or bank workers, beggars or college students, tailors or pavement artists."

books.title: Confessions of an Economic Hit Man
books.author: John Perkins
books.review:
John Perkins rips the heart of America and the drudgery. In one of the most riveting reads he explains the rise of oil thirsty corporates and politicians who wreck havoc in today's society. Mr.Perkin's assignments in the Latin countries and the ousting of various democratically elected leaders by the CIA explains a terrifying position and a new dimension the America of today has taken. A foreign policy solely based on its threats to other countries and invasions in the names of communists has made the USA an EMPIRE in its own right. It has become an Empire that adopts more subtle methods to make its agenda clear and carry out its vested interests in these areas.

Burdening various countries with debt and death alike, Mr.Perkins has explained his clever role today's beastly lot have taken up. A must read to understand the position of America in today's oil depleting world in the immense threat it poses for the future generations. If this does not stop and stop quick, it will lead to unexplainable consequences.

However, it remains to be answered if the world will open its eyes to the methods of rogue America.

books.title: First Among Equals
books.author: Jeffrey Archer
books.review:
Many consider First Among Equals Archer's finest. Some say that it has the necessary elements to make it better than Kane and Abel or Sons of Fortune. Personally, this book was a fine political novel and one could not have asked for a better description on the floor of the House of Commons.

Read it once you have a good understanding of British politics and parliamentary procedures. Archer manages to keep us puzzled and not until the last two words will you find out who the PM of Britain is. A fine pleasant read.

books.title: Maus I: Un Survivant Raconte: Mon Père Saigne L'histoire
books.author: Art Spiegelman

books.title: American Gods
books.author: Neil Gaiman
books.review: I know this is a classic. But i liked the initial 200 pages. Then I just gave up. Not my cup of tea, not my idea of fiction. Good writing nevertheless.

books.title: Life & Times of Michael K
books.author: J.M. Coetzee
books.review:
Coetzee masterly outlines mankind's basic rights in this masterly novel. A lot has been said about this masterpiece which catapulted him to a Nobel winning author.

Read it for the basic axiom it lays out - freedom and the right to choose is far more important than life itself. An emotive journey, Michael K is a solemn read documenting the troubles and rights of Africans. Powerful and captivating, its a grim tale of one man's beliefs and the lengths he will take to guard it.

Recommended - Read it in a sitting.

books.title: The Tipping Point: How Little Things Can Make a Big Difference
books.author: Malcolm Gladwell

books.title: As the Crow Flies
books.author: Jeffrey Archer
books.review: Disappointed. Flimsy plot, bad characterization and a long winding read. If you've read Kane and Abel or Sons of Fortune, this book will leave you aghast with shoddy writing. Best to ignore this one and move on to some of Archer's better works.

books.title: The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy (Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy, #1)
books.author: Douglas Adams

books.title: Brave New World
books.author: Aldous Huxley
books.review:
Put it in your shelf of MUST READS! Do not read it when you are very happy, do not read it when you are very sad. Huxley paints a dystopian world that we are fast approaching. IN this shocking literary masterpiece he takes you through a journey of psychedelic drugs and a world where 'love' is a taboo. Haven't we heard that before?

Shocking. Mesmerixing and painful. He does it all.

books.title: The Broker
books.author: John Grisham
books.review: Average plot. Substandard story. Very unlike Grisham. Be warned. Stay away from this one.

books.title: Kafka on the Shore
books.author: Haruki Murakami
books.review:
Murakami's crisp language and choice of words makes Kafka on the Shore a pleasant read. He explores various themes like wars, personal lives of authors and society at large. Through his characters he talks about his understanding of symbolism and post-modernism. Many have dubbed it as a modern Greek tragedy.

I must say that I was a tad disappointed after reading his short story; The 100% perfect girl. The book comes to a sudden halt leaving many questions unanswered. I later learnt that much of the Japanese readers have faced the same dilemma and the publisher received 8,000 odd questions of which Murakami answered 1,200 of them.

Kafka on the shore is easy and a simple read but in my opinion not one of Murakami's fortresses. The humor is kept minimum and the only strong point is the use of language. Read it if you must.

books.title: Open City
books.author: Teju Cole
books.review:
Anybody who follows Teju Cole on twitter, will be aware of his penchant with crafting clever sentences and his uncanny ability to present the most macabre news in a jovial 140 character limit. The Nigerian author is famous for his tweets called 18small fates 19 , Examples --

 1CNobody shot anybody, 1D the Abuja police spokesman confirmed, after the driver Stephen, 35, shot by Abuja police, almost died.

Knowledge is power. He graduated in business administration in Calabar,and Charles Okon has since administered sixteen armed robberies.

The 140 character limit acts as a constraint, yet is the true test for a journalist to condense information that has relevance and the required punch. I picked up Open City after reading a number of Cole 19s tweets convinced that his book will be filled with lip smacking sentences, and powerful stories. I was disappointed.

The Independent describes Cole 19s book as an 1Cexhilarating 1D post-melting-pot novel. Cole 19s book is anything but exhilarating. It 19s about a young Nigerian doctor 19s rant about everything, yet nothing. The character, Julius, glances over history, politics and bird migration, just as any commoner would do, but doesn't present a radical view nor engages the reader. Simply put, it 19s just a random conversation of things we already know.

While the book might be illuminating to a 11th grade kid who wants to know why Israel and Palestine are fighting, it serves no purpose for literary enlightenment or incisive knowledge. A thorough Wikipedia read should suffice.

Like history and politics, the book also touches on human behaviour but doesn't offer to take sides, delve into specific details, offer a chance to learn and understand something new, anything illuminating.

At best, Cole 19s novel is mash-up of everyday conversations on random topics. Not only is it a cumbersome read, the only thing I learnt from the book is how incessantly pestering bedbugs can be, much like the protagonist 19s never-ending narration.

Bottomline: Follow Teju Cole on twitter, he provokes you, engages you, is funny, witty and his crafting of sentences will leave you spell-bound. Just don 19t read his book.

books.title: The Finkler Question
books.author: Howard Jacobson
books.review:
Average book. Started well. Promised to be a humorous book with witty lines and characters with compassion. Failed miserably as it progressed. The Finkler Question is what Arundathi Roy's God of Small Things was to the Booker. Nonsense. While Roy's book was a bunch of metaphors with loose characters, Jacobson's is a bunch of funny statements woven around a hopeless story. Oh, and they both had loose characters.

Stay away from this one or read the reviews of The Guardian and The Independent and fall prey to Jacobson feigning artistic pleasures.

books.review:
A heart rendering book on a man who stood by his conscience and paid for it. Adiga's book was always supposed to be the lesser loved one after the stupendous success of The White Tiger. He touches on simple and common issues that plague today's Mumbai.

In a story that resonates with the manner of development that India has embarked on. The desperation of people and the ever so hungry need for money as the only means to happiness is well articulated.

The book coerces us to introspect on our values and what an India will look like in a few years. Read it for the good language, simple story and mild doses of humour.

books.title: India Since Independence: Making Sense of Indian Politics
books.author: V. Krishna Ananth
books.review:
The author makes it very clear that the book aims at getting many misguided facts right on Indian politics. The Indian political literati is filled with opinionated books on different parties, people and events. Krishna Ananth's book is a dry factual account of India Since Independence.

Written as a strictly factual journalistic account, the book lacks the emotion and opinion to empathize with the Indian political drama. It instead caters to aspiring students who want to understand the dynamics of Indian polity since Independence till 1991.

Krishna Ananth's knowledge is immense and the book should be treated as a political encyclopedia. I can't say I enjoyed reading it, but, I can proudly say that I understand politics and politicians rise much better.

It would take great difficulty to venture past 100 pages because of the dry writing. But, once you succeed, politics becomes a lot easier to comprehend. After all, one can't understand the sustenance of the Congress or any other party if they do not know about the political brinkmanship since Independence.

Recommended for political enthusiasts, students, researchers, journalists.

books.title: The Sense of an Ending
books.author: Julian Barnes
books.review:
Definitely not The Booker, but definitely a book rich in language and humor. Sometimes, you will have to judge a book because of its plaudits and Barnes' fine work will be assessed for its exalted Booker tag.

The sense of an ending takes you through the journey of a boy to a man in roughly 150 pages. It starts of with the classic humor of childhood misdemeanors and gets a tad boring in the middle only to end with the adrenaline rush of a crime mystery.

The title of the book syncs beautifully with the ending and leaves you shocked - I went back and read the 3 pages again.

Read it for its language, humor and above all Julian barnes' uniquely classy phrases.

books.title: The Last Wave
books.author: Pankaj Sekhsaria
books.review:
This is an important story. This is a story that needs to be heard. And for that alone it deserves 4 stars.

Pankaj disguises his historical account of the Jarawas in a readable 300 page book. The tale revolves around few characters but the real story is about the slow destruction of the Jarawa tribe in the Andamans. It packs in a lot of history and factual information on how the Jarawas are being marginalised. It also speaks about the lackadaisical style of governance in a slumbering island.

The Andamans is where civil servants are sent as a punishment and that explains the island's importance. Tourism is everything in the island. It has nothing else to offer and is home to the poorest people. For tourists, Sekshsaria's book brings to light the many daily problems the inhabitants of the island face. More importantly, it speaks about how we have grown apathetic to one of the world's most ancient and untouched civilisations.

The Jarawas are being modernised and we're interfering with the traditions. In an irony of sorts, inhabitants are the real colonialists and that's the story of the tribe. The Last Wave is a desperate attempt to urge everyone to think beyond the pristine beaches of the Andamans. It's a clarion call to the continent to help live and let live. And for that reason alone, it needs to be read. Or at least skimmed through.

books.title: The Sympathizer (The Sympathizer, #1)
books.author: Viet Thanh Nguyen
books.review:
Electric prose, but the last 50 pages were pointless and meandering. There's no real, discernible storyline in The Sympathizer.

 It's masterful writing, a profound reading of war, its people and the consequences of power in those who want to profit from it.

If there ever was a book on 'identity' politics, and the puzzling rhetoric of loyalties with nation states, this book has it all.

It can be supremely frustrating, hilarious, profound, deep, irritating, all in one. This is that book - one that'll make you want to throw it out of the window, but also cajole you into finishing it all.

Did I like it? Yes. No. Well, yes. No. 😊

books.title: Children of Time (Children of Time, #1)
books.author: Adrian Tchaikovsky
books.review:
I don't read much science fiction, or particularly enjoy reading this genre, but I'm beginning to think I've been missing out.

Children of Time was recommended to me at least ten times by a friend after I finished The Three-Body Problem. I finally picked it up on a trip to Indinesia, and boy, am I glad I did. I almost resented the fact that it made me want to do nothing else and keep reading instead of enjoying the trip.

This book is astonishing. The imagination, the ambition, the sheer conceptual brilliance. I still can't believe it made me care deeply about spiders, of all things, and built an entire world around them that felt utterly believable.

It features some of the finest world-building I've ever encountered. But what surprised me even more was the prose, the sheer deftness of the labguage and the gift of garb. There are beautiful passages, unforgettable lines, and moments of genuine literary elegance throughout.

This is not mereky some great science fiction novel. It's a beautifully written novel, that demands your attention. I fell in love with the characters, the world, and the writing. Every page radiates intelligence, curiosity, and craftsmanship.

This is a book to savor and be stunned with.
One of my favorite reads of 2026, and one I'd recommend wholeheartedly to anyone, even if you don't usually read science fiction.

books.author: Cho Nam-Joo
books.review:
A friend told me she switches on the lights only 5 minutes after entering her home, because she doesn't want people to know which apartment she stays in.

I couldn't empathise then. And as I read the pages of Kim Jiyoung, Born 1982, I realise what she truly meant.

It's a tough book to relate to, because as a male, we take a lot of things for granted, and realise how there's an endless list of 'privileges' we're so easily afforded. Being cognisant of these, are the best outcome of this work.

books.title: Butter
books.author: Asako Yuzuki
books.review:
Butter is best described as a self-help book masquerading as fiction.

It begins with tantalizing descriptions of food that make you want to rush into the kitchen and try the recipes yourself. But as the novel progresses, it becomes increasingly frustrating to read. The prose feels convoluted, perhaps because of the translation, but more importantly, the book meanders. It brushes up against misogyny, dabbles in feminism, and ultimately serves up a muddled, incoherent soup of ideas that never quite comes together.

What frustrated me most was that this supposedly fictional novel spends hundreds of pages building an intriguing, suspenseful plot, only to abandon it in the end. Rather than committing to a resolution, it asks the reader to look inward, make peace with ambiguity, and find their own answers.
Well, fuck that.

Tell me the ending. Tell me the story. Give me drama, suspense, or even a cliffhanger. But don't spend an entire novel building narrative tension only to shrug it off in favor of introspection. If you want to write philosophy, write philosophy. If you want to write fiction, commit to the story.

Disappointed

books.title: The Fifth Hour - The Moment You Can't Escape
books.author: Rahul Jain
books.review:
Every once in a while, I take a recommendation from a stranger because they swear by a book. More often than not, I'm disappointed. This is one of those books.
I finished it in two hours, and I want every one of those two hours back.
It's flimsy, random, and poorly written pop fiction. There was so much potential here, but I'll give the author the benefit of the doubt for at least putting a piece of work out into the world.
The only time I'd recommend this book is to someone stuck in a miserable reading slump who needs something very short and packed with enough masala to get them reading again.
Beyond that, it's a pass from me.
We need better books and better writing. That means spending more time researching, crafting better sentences, and searching for the right words than what this book offers.
